content: Nursing in the United Kingdom has a rich history, with its modern form largely attributed to Florence Nightingale. She established nursing schools in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, revolutionizing the profession. By the latter part of the 20th century, nursing evolved from being seen as a subordinate role to doctors to becoming a profession of independent practitioners with increased autonomy and professional status. Nurses now work in diverse settings, including hospitals, health centers, nursing homes, and patients' homes. The majority of nurses in the UK, nearly 400,000, are employed by the National Health Service (NHS) and are registered with the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC). Florence Nightingale is widely regarded as the founder of modern nursing. Before her time, there were no formal hospital training schools for nurses until one was established in Kaiserswerth, Germany, in 1846. Nightingale trained there and later founded the first nursing school at St. Thomas' Hospital in London, focusing on training nurses rather than merely providing hospital services. During the Crimean War in 1854, she was appointed to oversee the introduction of female nurses into British military hospitals in Turkey. Despite initial resistance from doctors, her team of 38 nurses became indispensable within days due to the influx of casualties. After the war, she withdrew from public life but continued to contribute significantly to healthcare reform and statistical analysis. In 1860, she became the first woman elected as a fellow of the Statistical Society. The history of nursing dates back to ancient times when care for the sick was often associated with spiritual practices. In early Christian eras, women in the church provided nursing care, often in patients' homes, gaining skills through experience rather than formal training. The religious roots of nursing are still evident in the UK today, with terms like Sister used for senior female nurses. Calls for state regulation of nursing began in the mid-19th century, paralleling the regulation of the medical profession. By the 1880s, organizations like the Hospitals Association advocated for nurse registration, though debates over training length and standards persisted. Florence Nightingale opposed formal regulation, believing essential nursing qualities could not be taught or regulated. The First World War significantly influenced nursing, with many unmarried women dedicating their lives to the profession. The College of Nursing was founded in 1915, and the Nurses Registration Act of 1919 established the General Nursing Council, formalizing the profession. Ethel Bedford-Fenwick became the first nurse on the English register. Over the decades, nursing roles expanded, and training standards evolved. By the 1920s, examinations were introduced for nurse registration, and the role of the sister tutor was created. The discovery of penicillin in 1928 and its subsequent civilian use in the 1940s transformed healthcare, including nursing practices. The NHS, launched in 1948, provided free, comprehensive healthcare and became the primary employer of nurses in the UK. The 1950s saw an influx of Caribbean nurses into British training programs and advancements in mental health nursing with the introduction of tranquilizers. Male nurses were integrated into the main nursing register in 1951. The 1960s brought sterile supplies, ending the need for nurses to sterilize equipment, and the first nursing degree program was introduced in Edinburgh. The Salmon Report of 1967 reformed nurse grading and management structures, and the first hospice was established by Dame Cicely Saunders. The 1970s and 1980s were marked by significant reforms and activism. Nurses demanded better pay and working conditions, leading to salary increases. The Royal College of Nursing became a trade union, and the Nursing Process emphasized assessment, planning, implementation, and evaluation in care. The Briggs Committee recommended changes to nurse training and regulation, culminating in the Nurses, Midwives, and Health Visitors Act of 1979. The UK Central Council for Nursing, Midwifery, and Health Visiting (UKCC) was established in 1983, overseeing professional standards and education until it was replaced by the NMC in 2002. Nursing education transitioned from hospital-based training to university programs under Project 2000. Pre-registration programs now require a degree or diploma, with specialized branches in adult, child, mental health, and learning disabilities nursing. Post-registration education is mandatory, with nurses required to complete 35 hours of education every three years. Many pursue advanced clinical skills or higher academic qualifications, such as master's degrees or PhDs, to specialize further or take on roles like nurse consultants or educators. The NHS employs the majority of UK nurses, categorized into registered and non-registered staff. Non-registered staff, such as healthcare assistants, provide direct patient care under supervision. Registered nurses are divided into first-level nurses, who form the bulk of the workforce, and second-level nurses, whose training is no longer provided but who can still practice. Specialist nurses, including nurse practitioners and clinical nurse specialists, often work at advanced practice levels, providing leadership, education, and specialized care. Some nurses transition into management roles within the NHS, while others focus on clinical education and research. The NMC maintains a register of nurses, midwives, and specialist community public health nurses, ensuring professional standards and public protection. As of 2005, there were over 672,000 registered nurses in the UK, with more than 10% being male. The NMC's core functions include setting standards for education and practice, handling misconduct complaints, and ensuring quality in nursing and midwifery education. The title registered nurse is legally protected, and practitioners must hold valid registration with the NMC to practice lawfully in the UK.
